Modal Verbs (Review)
Modal verbs allow you to express ability, obligation, desire, and permission to do something when you use them with other verbs.

Can

You use this modal verb to talk about possibilities, abilities, and requests (informal). In order to develop ideas including the modal verb “can,” you need to use the following structure:

Subject + modal verb(can) + main verb in base form + complement


In negative sentences, you place the “not” adverb after the modal verb.

Examples:

Class diagrams can display interactions between objects.
Structure diagrams cannot/can't be used for this project.

Should

This modal verb is used to give suggestions and advice. In order to develop ideas including the modal verb “should,” you need to use the following structure:

Subject + Modal verb (should) + main verb in base form + complement


In negative sentences, you use Not after Should.

Examples:
We should use a more detailed behavior diagram.
They shouldn't/should not rely so much on drafts for modeling software.

Superlatives
You can use Superlatives to talk about a noun that the highest degree of a quality.

In order to use superlatives with short adjectives, you need to use the definite article The, and the adjective with the -est suffix. Remember, short adjectives have only one or two syllables.

Examples:

The fastest way to develop software is by using the appropriate modeling tool. (fast)
Digital tools offer the simplest approach to software modeling. (simple)

Note: There are a few exceptions to this rule. With irregular adjectives, the superlative form changes. Here are a few examples:

What is a Diagram?
A diagram is a graphic representation of something. Sometimes, you can also refer to them using the word Graph.

In software design, planning and development, diagrams help engineers and designers to have a draft of the set of instructions, commands, and actions that a piece of software can have. </br></br>  UML is a standardized way of making software development diagrams. There are many of them, each one serving a different purpose depending on the designer's needs. However, diagrams in UML are divided into two major groups, which are Structural, Behavior and Interaction. </br></br>  Among structural ones, you can find Class, deployment, object, package and profile diagrams. This kind presents the information that must be included in the system as well as the structure it must have. </br></br>  Behavior diagrams show the actions that need to occur within the system, as well as its functionality. Interaction diagrams are considered to be a part of behavioral ones, and they focus more on control and dataflow.

Tanner: So, Justin can we please review the information we have about class diagrams?
Justin: Of course, Tanner! We should do that, because we have the longest exam next week!
Tanner: Okay, I can see in my notes that class diagrams can show a static view of the system by displaying the classes, particular attributes, behaviors, operations, and interactions between objects. It's one of the most popular modeling standards in UML. In this kind of models, a class refers to the attributes and behaviors that objects can generate. It also contains possible messages, constraints, stereotypes or tagged values within the object.

Justin: I see. We should try to identify their key features; that is the fastest way to understand them. There's plenty of information online!
Tanner: Definitely. It's important to note that class diagrams can show a static structure of the software; it doesn't take time into account. The clearest way to make use of these diagrams is to present system types, instances, and the way they should relate and interact. We can even see the internal structure of those classes in a hierarchy.

Justin: That's one of the easiest definitions of class diagrams! Another characteristic is that we can display classes in boxes that have three sections; the first one has the name, the second one includes the attributes of the class, and the last one has the operations that the class can execute.
Tanner: One of the attributes of these diagrams is that, by showing relationships, there are conditions or operations that we need to complete for objects to interact.
Justin: I also see that the strongest advantage of these diagrams is when designers need to document the system's code, because they present a solid foundation for defining tasks and workflow.
Tanner: Should we keep looking for more information?
Justin: No, I think we're ready for that exam now!
